idiom_name: single-member struct strong typedef (typedef struct { uint32_t value; } user_id_t;)
implementation_notes: C has no distinct-type facility: typedef is a transparent alias, so two typedefs of the same primitive stay interchangeable and the compiler cannot help. The local realization is a struct with exactly one member - the tag gives user_id_t and order_id_t different types, so a bare integer or the other id does not convert implicitly - plus hand-written functions for construction, the accessor and equality, because C has neither struct comparison nor methods. Keep validation in the constructor function (user_id_from) and treat the .value member as private by convention: nothing in the language stops other translation units from bypassing it, so a header discipline ('only this type's functions touch the member') is part of the pattern here.
pitfalls: C cannot compare structs with == or memcmp portably (padding bytes), so every wrapper needs its own equality function; using memcmp is a classic latent bug.
The anonymous form typedef struct { ... } x_t; cannot be forward-declared - use the tagged form (typedef struct x_t { ... } x_t;) when the type appears in headers or circular references.

The member is reachable from any translation unit that sees the definition, so the 'private' representation is a convention: keep the struct definition out of public headers (opaque handle) where the boundary permits.
